name: Delphi 5/6/7
title: Object Pascal and the VCL
intro: Delphi paired the Object Pascal language with a form designer: drop a button on a window, double-click it, and type what should happen. Versions 5, 6 and 7 were the classic Windows releases, and Delphi 7 in particular stayed in use for years. This course teaches the language with small console programs first, then classes, exceptions and finally forms. To run the console programs, choose File → New → Other → Console Application in Delphi, or use Free Pascal (fpc -Mdelphi file.pas) or the Lazarus IDE, which run almost the same code today on Windows, Linux and macOS. Every console example shows exactly what it prints.

sections.p: A console program starts with program Name;. {$APPTYPE CONSOLE} tells Delphi to open a text window. Variables are declared with their types in a var block before begin. Assignment is :=; a single = compares. Statements are separated by semicolons, and the program ends with end. (with a full stop).
WriteLn prints its arguments one after another and then starts a new line; Write stays on the same line. Text goes in single quotes; to put a quote inside, double it.
// comments to the end of the line. { ... } and (* ... *) can cover several lines. A brace followed by $, like {$APPTYPE CONSOLE}, is not a comment but an instruction to the compiler.
Pascal ignores upper and lower case in names: WriteLn, writeln and WRITELN are the same, and so are nuts and Nuts. Delphi programmers usually write keywords in lower case and names in CamelCase.

practice.q: How do you assign 5 to x?
practice.why: Pascal uses := for assignment and = for comparison.
Write does not start a new line, so all three letters share one line.
The main block ends with end and a full stop; other blocks end with end;.
a becomes 4 × 4, and WriteLn puts the number straight after the text.

options: In a var block before begin
practice.answer: In a var block before begin
practice.why: Pascal wants every variable named, with its type, before the code that uses it.

practice.q: How do you write the text Don't in Pascal?
practice.why: Strings use single quotes, and a quote inside is written twice.
A doubled quote inside a string becomes one quote in the output.

options: Opens a text window for WriteLn
practice.answer: Opens a text window for WriteLn
practice.why: It is a compiler directive that makes a console program instead of a GUI one.

lessons.title: Types and formatting
lessons.summary: Integer, Double, Boolean, Char and string; constants and Format.

sections.p: Every variable has a fixed type. The everyday ones are Integer (whole numbers), Double (decimals), Boolean (True or False), Char (one character) and string. Putting text into an Integer is a compile error, not a surprise at run time.

/ always gives a Double. For whole numbers use div (division without remainder) and mod (the remainder). To print a Double neatly, add a width and a number of decimals: x:0:2 means “as wide as needed, two decimals”.
A const block names values that never change. The compiler works out their type.

IntToStr and StrToInt convert between numbers and text; they live in the SysUtils unit, which the uses line brings in. Format fills a pattern: %d for an integer, %s for a string, %.2f for a decimal with two places.
sections.out:
Total: 42
24
Hazel has 12 nuts weighing 0.50 kg

sections.p: Ord gives a character's code and Chr turns a code back into a character. Inc and Dec add or take one.

practice.why: div is whole-number division; mod would give the remainder, 2.
6 fits into 20 three times with 2 left over.
/ gives a Double, and :0:1 prints it with one decimal.
3 > 4 is false; WriteLn spells Booleans in capitals.

practice.q: What happens with x: Integer; x := 'five';?
practice.why: Pascal checks types when it compiles, so a string cannot go into an Integer.
Format replaces %d with the integer and %s with the string, in order.
Inc moves A to B, and Ord(B) is 66.
IntToStr turns 12 into digits with no spaces, then + joins them to the text.

lessons.title: Decisions
lessons.summary: if/then/else, begin…end blocks, and/or/not, and case.

sections.p: if condition then statement else statement. To do several things, wrap them in begin … end. There is no semicolon before else: the whole if/else is one statement.
and and or bind more tightly than comparisons, so each comparison needs its own brackets: (age > 9) and (age < 20). Not-equal is <>.
case picks a branch by an ordinal value: an integer, a character or an enumeration (not a string). Branches can list values and ranges.
c in ['a'..'z'] tests whether a character is in a set, which is shorter than several comparisons.

practice.q: What is wrong with: if x > 1 then WriteLn('a'); else WriteLn('b');
practice.why: A semicolon ends the if statement, so the else has nothing to belong to.
The first test fails, the second passes, and the rest is skipped.

options: and binds tighter than >, so it would try 1 and b first
and only works on Booleans in brackets
practice.answer: and binds tighter than >, so it would try 1 and b first
practice.why: Without brackets Pascal reads a > (1 and b) > 1, which is not what you meant.
6 is in the list 6, 7.

practice.q: Which can a case statement switch on?
practice.why: case needs an ordinal type: integers, characters, Booleans or enumerations.
n equals 4, so not (n = 3) is true.
Q sits in the range Q to Z.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: for to/downto, while, repeat…until, Break and Continue.

sections.p: for counts with to or downto, one step at a time. The loop variable must be a local ordinal variable, and you must not change it inside the loop.
sections.out:
1 is odd
2 is even
3 is odd
3 2 1 go!

sections.p: while tests before each round, so it may run zero times. repeat … until tests after, so it always runs at least once, and it needs no begin … end.
Break leaves the loop at once. Continue skips the rest of this round and goes on to the next.

A variable outside the loop collects a result. Set it to 0 first. Variables in the main program's var block start at 0, but variables declared inside a procedure or function start with whatever happened to be in memory, so setting them is a good habit everywhere.

practice.why: The loop includes both ends, and Write adds no spaces.
The test fails straight away, so the body never runs.
repeat runs the body once before testing.
Break leaves the loop as soon as i reaches 3.

practice.q: Why set total := 0 before the loop?
options: Variables inside routines do not start at 0 by themselves
practice.answer: Variables inside routines do not start at 0 by themselves
practice.why: Pascal does not clear variables declared in a procedure or function, so they hold leftover values until you set them.
Continue skips the even numbers, and Write adds no spaces.
downto counts 3, 2, 1 and the sum is 6.

lessons.title: Procedures and functions
lessons.summary: Result, parameters by value, var and const, and local variables.

sections.p: A procedure does something; a function returns a value by assigning to the built-in Result variable. They are declared before the main begin, and can have their own var block.
Normally a routine gets a copy of each argument. Mark a parameter var and it works on the caller's own variable instead. const promises not to change it, which lets Delphi skip the copy for strings.
Exit leaves a routine straight away. In a function, set Result first: whatever it holds is the answer.
A function can call itself, as long as some case stops it.

practice.q: How does a function hand back its value?
practice.why: Every Delphi function has an implicit Result variable.
The inner call gives 6 and the outer call doubles it.
A var parameter is the caller's own variable, so a becomes 0.
Without var the procedure works on a copy; a is untouched.

practice.q: What does const in front of a parameter promise?
options: The routine will not change it
practice.answer: The routine will not change it
practice.why: The compiler refuses changes, and can avoid copying large values.
7 + 5 is 12, then the if caps Result at 10.

practice.q: How do you declare a procedure that can change the caller's Integer?
practice.why: var before the parameter makes it the caller's own variable.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Indexing from 1, Length, Copy, Pos, Insert, Delete and case.

sections.p: Unlike most languages, the first character of a Delphi string is at index 1. Length gives the size and Copy(s, start, count) takes a piece. + joins strings.
Pos(sub, s) gives where sub starts in s, or 0. Insert and Delete change a string variable in place. UpperCase, LowerCase and Trim come from SysUtils.
A for loop from 1 to Length(s) visits every character. Here it counts the vowels.
StringOfChar repeats a character, and a loop can build a string one piece at a time.

practice.why: Delphi strings are indexed from 1.
Starting at character 6 (n), take three: n, u, t.
w is 1, a is 2, l is 3.
Delete removes four characters starting at 1: p, i, n, e.
The space counts as a character.
Insert puts hazel at position 1, in front of nut.
StringOfChar repeats the character the given number of times.

lessons.title: Arrays and records
lessons.summary: Fixed and dynamic arrays, Low and High, and records.

sections.p: A static array has its index range in its type: array[1..5] of Integer. Low and High give the first and last index, so loops do not need the numbers written twice.
array of Integer has no fixed size. SetLength sizes it, and it always counts from 0.
A record groups named fields into one type. Arrays of records are how many Delphi programs hold their data.
A typed constant can hold a whole table, which is handy for lookups.

practice.q: What does High return for array[1..5] of Integer?
practice.why: High is the last index in the declared range.

practice.q: What is the first index of a dynamic array?
practice.why: Dynamic arrays always count from 0; static arrays use the range you declare.
v[3] is 9 and v[2] is 4.
Three items numbered 0, 1 and 2.

practice.q: How do you read the Nuts field of the record in team[1]?
practice.why: Pick the element first, then the field with a dot.
Low and High return the declared bounds of a static array.
The fields hold 3 and 4, and 3 × 4 is 12.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Fields, methods, constructors, properties, inheritance and Free.

sections.p: A class bundles data (fields) with the code that works on it (methods). Objects are created with a constructor, usually Create, and must be freed with Free when you are done. try … finally makes sure the Free happens even if something goes wrong.

Fields start with F by convention and are kept private. The outside world uses properties, which can read a field directly or call a method. A property with no write is read-only. Object fields start at 0, empty or nil, unlike local variables.
A class can extend another. A method marked virtual can be replaced in a descendant with override; then calling it through a variable of the parent type runs the right version for each object.
obj is TOwl asks whether an object is a TOwl (or a descendant). obj as TOwl treats it as one, and raises an error if it is not.
sections.code:
if zoo[i] is TOwl then
  WriteLn('An owl!');

practice.q: What frees an object you created with Create?
practice.why: Delphi objects are not garbage-collected; whoever creates one frees it, usually in a finally block.

options: It runs even if an error happens in the try part
practice.answer: It runs even if an error happens in the try part
practice.why: try … finally guarantees the clean-up code runs on every way out.
Object fields start at 0, and each Bump adds one.

options: Replaces a virtual method in a descendant class
practice.answer: Replaces a virtual method in a descendant class
practice.why: Calls through a parent-type variable then run the descendant's version.

practice.q: What is a property with read FName and no write?
practice.why: Without a write part, code outside the class can read the property but not set it.
b holds a TKid, so the override runs even though the variable's type is TBase.

practice.q: What does obj is TOwl ask?
options: Whether obj is a TOwl or a descendant
Whether obj has a Free method
practice.answer: Whether obj is a TOwl or a descendant
practice.why: is tests the object's real class at run time.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.summary: try…except, raise, and handling particular kinds of error.

sections.p: When something goes wrong, Delphi raises an exception: normal running stops and jumps to the nearest except block. on E: Exception do catches it and gives you the exception object, whose Message says what happened.
sections.out:
4 nuts is fine
Problem: Nuts cannot be negative
carrying on

sections.p: Exceptions are classes, so you can catch particular kinds. StrToInt raises EConvertError on bad text; div by zero raises EDivByZero. The first matching on wins.
sections.out:
abc: not a number
5: divided by zero

sections.p: Often you can avoid the exception: StrToIntDef(s, 0) gives 0 instead of raising. Keep try … except for problems you cannot check in advance, and try … finally for clean-up.

practice.why: raise Exception.Create('...') creates and raises an exception.
raise jumps straight to except, so c is never printed.
seven is not written in digits, so the default -1 is returned.

practice.q: What is the difference between except and finally?
options: except handles errors; finally always runs
finally handles errors; except always runs
practice.answer: except handles errors; finally always runs
practice.why: Use except to deal with a problem and finally to clean up whatever happens.
except catches the raise, prints the Message, then the program carries on.
'12' converts to 12; 'x' is not a number so the default 3 is used.

sections.p: Each form is a unit with two halves: interface (what other units can see) and implementation (the code). The form designer writes the class declaration for you as you drop components on it. A form is a class, just like the ones in the last lessons.

Double-clicking Button1 in the designer creates Button1Click and connects it to the button's OnClick event. The layout itself is saved in the .dfm file, which {$R *.dfm} links in. Components are objects of VCL classes such as TButton, TEdit and TLabel, and their settings (Caption, Text, Enabled) are properties you can set in the Object Inspector or in code. The form owns its components and frees them when it closes.
Text boxes hold strings, so convert numbers on the way in and out. StrToIntDef copes with a box the user left empty.
Several buttons can share one OnClick handler. Sender says which was clicked, and as turns it into a TButton so you can read its Caption.

practice.q: Which file stores a form's layout?
practice.why: The .pas file holds the code; the .dfm holds the components and their properties.

practice.q: Which part of a unit can other units use?
practice.why: Only what is declared in the interface section is visible outside the unit.

practice.q: What does the Sender parameter of an event tell you?
practice.why: One handler can serve several buttons; Sender says which one was clicked.

practice.q: How do you show the number n in Label1?
practice.why: Caption is a string property, so the integer has to be converted.

practice.q: What does {$R *.dfm} do in a form unit?
options: Links the form's layout resource into the program
practice.answer: Links the form's layout resource into the program
practice.why: The .dfm is compiled as a resource and {$R *.dfm} pulls it in.

practice.q: How do you show a short message box?
practice.why: ShowMessage (from Dialogs) pops up a simple modal box with OK.

lessons.title: Putting it together: FizzBuzz
lessons.summary: Loops, mod, a function and string building in one program.

sections.p: FizzBuzz counts from 1, but says Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5 and FizzBuzz for both. Building the word inside a function keeps the main loop short, and an empty result means “just say the number”.
sections.out: 1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz

sections.p: You have the core of Object Pascal. Good next steps: turn FizzBuzz into a form with a button and a TMemo that fills with lines; use TStringList (in the Classes unit) to load, sort and save text files; and read the VCL source that ships with Delphi, which is written in exactly the language you now know.

practice.why: 9 divides by 3 and 10 divides by 5.

practice.q: Why does Say start with Result := ''?
options: So the later tests add to a known value
practice.answer: So the later tests add to a known value
practice.why: Result + 'Buzz' needs Result to hold something definite first, so the function sets it before testing.
IntToStr gives the digits with no spaces.
15 is a multiple of both 3 and 5; 7 matches neither so it stays a number.
14 matches neither test; 15 gets Fizz then Buzz joined.
